projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with George Schlee was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: George Schlee
sp.p: In Cleveland.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum. How old were you?

sp.speaker: George Schlee
sp.p: I was 16 years old.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Still in school?

sp.speaker: George Schlee
sp.p: Yes. And I quit school when the war -- when Pearl Harbor was bombed to go to work, and I felt like I was helping that way better than going to school.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: George Schlee
sp.p: No, not really. It was scary, you know. It was big news. And in those days the paper kids ran down the street, you know, saying "Extra, extra", in Cleveland, especially, and you'd get a paper. A lot of people didn't have papers delivered to their homes, and -- and everybody was just in awe, you know. And that's really all I can remember about it. There weren't any -- There wasn't any TV, so we didn't see any pictures or anything, except later on in the newspaper, they had pictures of the destruction. But that was about it. And I -- I felt I wanted to be a Marine right then and there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So how soon after that did you quit school?

sp.speaker: George Schlee
sp.p: Well, I -- Let's see. I finished my semester and then in the beginning of '42 I quit. I quit, and I was in 11th grade.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And where did you go to work then?

sp.speaker: George Schlee
sp.p: I went to work with my dad. He worked in a box factory on Scranton Road in Cleveland, and he got me a job as tail-off. A tail-off is somebody that accepts the wood after somebody pushes it through the saw. And I was the youngest one there, of course. I stayed there until I was 18. And I wanted to make sure I got in the Marine Corps, so a couple months before I was 18 I went to the recruiting office in Cleveland because I heard they weren't taking many Marines, they were taking -- they were picking what they wanted at the time, and I was going to be drafted, and I certainly didn't want to get in the Army, and so I went down there and they says, if you want to get in the Marine Corps so bad you'll get first crack at it the day you go down when you're drafted. So I says, okay. And out of 1500 guys they took 30 Marines, and I got first pick, so, then after that --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Why did you want to go in the Marines so badly?

sp.speaker: George Schlee
sp.p: I -- I don't know. I just felt like I wanted to be a tough guy or something. I don't know. I wanted to be the best. I heard it was the best, and I just wanted to do -- be in the best so, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: All right. So when did you actually go in then?

sp.speaker: George Schlee
sp.p: Well, I went in -- My birthday was in October, so I was drafted immediately, and at the end of October I was sent down to Paris Island boot camp in South Carolina, Paris Island, and I spent three months in boot camp, and then when I walked out of boot camp I felt like I was the best. They brain washed me down there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Would this be like October of '43 then?

sp.speaker: George Schlee
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So anything you can tell me about boot camp?

sp.speaker: George Schlee
sp.p: Well, it was tough. I was -- I only weighed about 140 pounds, and was almost six feet tall. I was a skinny guy, and I think that's what saved my life many times, being skinny. And I was good on the rifle range. I was good in marching. I took a beating one day when they pitted some guy up against me and boxed for 10 or 15 minutes. He beat the daylights out of me. And I didn't get into trouble. And I had a lot of pot walloping 'cause there was a lot of going on in boot camp.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Pot walloping?

sp.speaker: George Schlee
sp.p: Yeah, cleaning pots in the mess hall. I ate good; they had good food. And I excelled in the bayonet course in marksmanship, and so when I got out I -- In fact, our drill instructor, we could see tears in his eyes when we graduated because -- I don't know whether we were an exceptional platoon that he had drilled, so he was proud of us. And so we got brainwashed, of course, and when I put my first set of greens on with that leather belt. They had leather belts and brass buckles then, they don't have them now. And when I walked out of there I just felt like a million bucks. And then we went home. They gave you a leave for two weeks, and I went home and showed myself off at home to my girlfriends. There was no problem having girlfriends with a uniform on in World War II. So then after that was -- They send me back to Camp Lejeune in North Carolina for advanced training. And I guess they picked me for artillery. I don't know why. I don't know how they pick your MOS, but I thought, well, okay. So I was there for about a month and a half. They were shoving us through as fast as they could. I think the training would have been longer. I had a tough time in the -- in the obstacle course. I was a lousy climber, and I couldn't climb rope. I couldn't do it in high school in gym. I got through but I just had a hard time. There was a funny thing that happened to us one day in Camp Lejeune there. We had a warrant officer, and he came over to our barracks on a Sunday. We had the day off on Sundays, and he was in his full dress uniform. And all of the guys weren't even in the barracks. And he says, "Everybody out. Line up out here, front and center." And we says, you know, what's wrong with this guy. And he was half in the bag; he'd been drinking. So we were only PFCs, so we thought, well, we better do what he says, you know. So we get our clothes on. Some of us were just in our underclothes. And he lined us all, and he says, "We're going to run the obstacle course." And we weren't too happy about that. So he gets us out there, and he's out there in his full dress running with us. He's leading us, in fact. But he got to the part where the rope was hanging above the dirty water, and he ran and missed it and plopped right in that dirty water with his dress uniform on. And he sat down in that water and he bust out laughing, and, of course, we all laughed too. It was the funniest thing we ever saw. And we helped him get out of there. I don't think he could stand up. And that was the end of the obstacle course when he got there, we never finished. And so we went back to the barracks and he brought us all a beer, and we had a great time with him. But that was funny. And I don't think too many guys would ever see something like that. After that then we got on a train, and went cross country to San Diego. We were in a -- We were secretly stuck into a little town or township or something called Linda Vista just outside of San Diego. We weren't allowed to make phone calls or anything. And then we were there for two or three days, and then they got us on a boat, and took us for a ride down to New Caledonia. And I was put into a replacement battalion. I think it was Replacement Battalion 54. And we weren't allowed to -- We were right at the end of the road. We were in a muddy area. The Army had a nice place farther up the road, and they were able to go to town. We were secretly kept at the end of the road in our area, and we couldn't do anything there. And, in fact, we were right next to the Marine raider's obstacle course. That's where their obstacle course was for their training. Well, we weren't there very long, a couple weeks. Then they put us on a ship. It was called the? Ros Chambeau(ph). It was a liner, a French liner, and I guess in its day it was a real nice ship, you know, luxury ship. Well, I think they packed 5,000 us on to that thing, and it seems like we were five holes deep. I know I was below the water line in my sack, and they had us about five sacks high, I think. We couldn't even sit up in our sacks. When we got to warmer -- nearer the equator on that boat we -- some of us just couldn't breathe down there. There was no air conditioning down there, and you couldn't feel any air either. So we tried to spend most of our time top side anywhere, laying on top of one another if we had to. And the ship had an escort for a certain amount of miles out of New Caledonia. Then I don't know whether the Navy was short of ships or something at that time. Of course, they took a big loss at Pearl Harbor. We had no escort. We -- General alarm was called several times, but -- and every time they did that we had to go down in the hole. They shoved us down there like cattle, you know, and then the crew had to man their gun positions. And we never knew what was going on in that top side. That bothered us. So one night it was real nice and warm, the sea was nice and smooth, and we were just rolling along there, and everybody was top side, and it was real warm. And general quarters was called, and nobody moved. We weren't going to go below. And some of our sergeants says, "Don't move." Says -- There's 5,000 of us on this ship. Well, the captain spoke over the loudspeaker and said -- I don't know what he all said, but he wasn't talking very nice to us, and he was going to do this to us, and mentioned mutiny, and all kinds of baloney, and we were all starting to laugh. And ESPs came around with their clubs, started hitting us on the end of our feet, telling us to go below, and we told them in so many words to go fly a kite. And so we stayed top side. And the ship broke down several times on the way over to Guadalcanal. That's where our destination was. And we were just sitting in the ocean there with no escort. And they'd get it started and sometimes it would fail. Then they'd get it started again, and I don't know, it must have been the grace of God that that ship made it down to Guadalcanal, but I understand afterwards it was -- they were taking it down to Australia, and that was the last trip it was going to make. I mean it was done for. But on this ship our officers were living like kings up there on top side in those suites and everything else. You know, they never converted them. I guess they had no time for that, and they shoved us down in the hole and made a quicky down there, you know, mounted all these sacks up. We only had two meals a day too. And you had to stand up to eat, of course. And in rough weather, why, you know, the pitcher of milk, if you didn't catch it when it went by, why, you had to wait for it to come back, and it might have been empty. So the food wasn't that great either aboard ship.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How long was that trip from New Caledonia to --

sp.speaker: George Schlee
sp.p: Boy, I can't remember. I don't know. I can't remember. Those kind of things I can't remember.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's all right.

sp.speaker: George Schlee
sp.p: And, well, when we got to Guadalcanal I was put into a palm tree area, and -- in a replacement battalion, and I was put in to an anti aircraft outfit on Guadalcanal. I thought, gee, this is going to be different because I thought the island was secured. When you're a PFC in war you don't know anything. I mean you're just a follower, and you do what you're told, and you don't know what the heck's going on. So we were put on the beach on 40 millimeters. They trained us, and they would fly a plane by with a sleeve on the end of a wire, a rope, and we were supposed to shoot at it, just boom, boom, boom, boom. Well, that lasted -- I don't know how long that lasted. I can't remember how long I was on Guadalcanal, but the thing was I think they were just doing -- putting us there to keep us busy because there were no enemy planes there. And there weren't any Marines on the island going out scouting for Japs either. Once in a while a stray one would show up and surrender or they catch one fishing on one of their rivers, you know. I was washing one day next to a little creek there, and I saw a Japanese helmet come floating down the creek in front of me. So -- So we were -- Oh, I'm sorry, I'll have to backtrack just -- I didn't go to -- I did land at Guadalcanal, yeah, okay. But shortly afterwards I wasn't -- Before I was put in the 40 millimeter anti-aircraft outfit, they hauled us aboard ship again and took us to an island 60 miles away from Guadalcanal called Pavuvu. And we did nothing there. We just were sitting in pyramidal tents, and I don't know -- 'cause we only stayed there for about a couple of weeks. Then we went back to Guadalcanal again. But on Pavuvu I met my first tarantula spider. I was -- It was at night. I was in my pyramidal tent. I didn't know any of the guys in my tent. They -- I guess they were guys that already been up to Cape Gloucester in the Solomons; they'd been fighting already. And so I'm sleeping there in -- and I look out and the moon's shining. I see this, it looked like a monster to me climbing up the edge of my mosquito net. I didn't know whether that thing was on the inside and the outside, and I wasn't going to touch it. So I said, what the heck am I going to do. So I jumped out of the other side of my mosquito net, and got off my cot. And everybody else in the tent was sleeping. So I woke one of the guys up, and I asked him if he had a flashlight. I didn't have one. And he says, no, he didn't. He says, "Nobody in here's got a flashlight." And so I wasn't going to go back in that sack. So I went outside in the pathway there in front of the tent city there, and I must have drifted off. I leaned against a tree or something, and I -- somebody woke me up in the morning. I was leaning against a tree. And they -- And the guys told me they killed a spider in the morning. They didn't know where I was. They didn't even know why I wasn't there, you know. I didn't tell them I saw a spider. So anyway back to the 40 millimeters on Guadalcanal. I think I did that for about a month, and everything was secret because I found out later that the Marine Corps was forming a Sixth Division. They normally had five, the Corps, and they didn't want the Japs to know that they were forming this division on Guadalcanal, 'cause Tokyo Rose would come through on the radio every once in a while and say, "I know where all you little Marine boneheads are. I'm going to find you," you know. And I don't know how they kept that secret. At least 20,000 guys training on an island like that, but I guess they did. And then they put me in the division, in a battalion, and I was in the 105 Artillery. Well, they come around -- I guess they didn't ask for volunteers in those days. So the lieutenant came to my tent one day while we were training, during training there, and he said, "Private Schlee." I says, "Yes, sir." He says, "You're going to be in a forward observing team." And I wasn't too happy about that. And he picked out about six guys, and I knew all of them, fortunately, so -- and one of them was, we called him Frenchie. He was Lou Boudreau, the baseball player's brother, a big husky guy. So when it was time to board, to go to, I don't know, I can't remember how long we trained, I just can't remember. You want to hear a couple things that happened before?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: George Schlee
sp.p: Oh, okay. Well, you know, we had lister bags for water, and they had little spigots at the bottom of them. And we usually got our water at night when it was cooler. And this one night I went over to the lister bag. I was filling up my canteen, and I heard a voice says, "Don't take anymore water." And I says, what the heck, where's the voice coming from. So I looked, and this guy was sitting in the lister bag in the water, and he says, "I'm taking a bath." I says, "You can't do that. You'll get in trouble." So I went and got a senior officer. And I says, "You know, I might have soapy water in my canteen. I'm not going to drink it." And I says, "This guy's in here taking a bath." And, of course, a lot of guys thought it was funny, but he was trying to get a Section 8 to get out, see, but it didn't work. And they put him on an FO team too. So that was his penalty. I didn't like that because he was being penalized being an FOT, and they didn't even ask me to volunteer. And we had another guy that was trying to get a Section 8 too. He kept walking around with an invisible frog, and he would tell the guys, you know, be careful when you walked, that you didn't step on his little frog. You know, like he had a leash on him, he would walk around like that. And nobody bothered him, you know. We thought it was funny, and then after a while -- I forgot what the frog's name was but we'd say hi to the frog, and the officers, they thought it was funny too, but he was harmless, and they probably had an idea that's what he was trying to do, you know, get, become a psychon and get shipped out, but that didn't work either. So when we were boarding -- Oh, another thing. When we unloaded ships, we'd get ship -- At night we would load some of the ships that came down at the Coquom (ph) docks down there at Guadalcanal. And sometimes they'd have beer, you know, and we found out that canned beer floats in salt water. So we would have a team of us there on the dock, and some of us would be underneath the dock, on the structure underneath, and the guys up top side would happen to miss the net, and a case of it would go into the water, and we'd drag it underneath there and get ourselves some free beer that way. Another way we got beer is we would get a six-by and some brave Marine would get on the hood of a six-by truck, and follow an Army vehicle hauling food and beer through the jungles there, and jump on the tailgate and before they noticed us, in fact, there, we'd have a few cartons of our -- or cases of beer off to the side of the road in the jungle there, and go back and pick it up, and we got beer and goodies that way too. So I can't think of anything else -- Well, we had an accident there one time. It wasn't funny. I guess some of the guys laughed about it later on, months later, but we had a 12-seater head up on this little knoll, and at night -- or at dusk somebody would go in there and throw kerosene seen down in the holes. We had a 12-seater up there, and set them on fire to burn them up so they didn't stink and that. Well, this guy threw gasoline in there by mistake, and he just blew that place up, and he went with it. And several people got hurt, but he went with it. And we -- Well, the funny part was, you know, we had turds on top of the pyramidal tents in some places, and that was the funny part. We had a turdy outfit for a while, so. Another thing I did when I boarded ship, we were given an allowance of beer in cans. And when I was on Guadalcanal I saved up 13 of them and I was going to drink them on my birthday. And so when I got 13 of them, and, of course, the beer was warm, and not having drank any beer for a long time, I got plastered, and I got sick and everything else, and that was the first and last time I ever did that. But when I knew I was going into combat and get on that ship, we had a horseshoe pack and -- that went around our regular pack, our blanket rolls, and I saved up ten cans of beer and I put them in that shoe, in my pack there in the U-shaped part of it. It made my pack a little heavier climbing up the net, but when I got aboard ship, well, we were out a couple of days, I found one of the crew -- Nobody knew I had that beer, I kept that a secret. One of the crew I discovered was -- Well, you go around asking people, you know, say, "Where you from?" See. And he says, I'm from Cleveland. I says, "I know you. You look like the paper boy we had at home." And he says, "Yeah. I delivered the Cleveland Press." I says, "Well, I lived on Woodbridge." He says, "Yeah, I did deliver to your house." So we got to be buddies aboard ship, and I told him I had some beer, and I traded him off some beer -- Well, we drank some together at night, of course, when nobody was around, or we found a spot where there wasn't anybody. And he got me a hammock. And I was on a regular troop ship. I think it was called the Jackson, one of those -- I can't think of the company, the guy that made cars.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Kaiser?

sp.speaker: George Schlee
sp.p: Kaisers, yeah, one of those that fell apart on the ocean I understand. And that's what I was on. And there was a little cubby hole there on deck, and he set this hammock up for me. It was three-sided, and then the ocean was right there by the rail. And I thought, holy smokes, I'm going to be living like a king on this boat. And my buddies were all envious of me, and I didn't, I was running out of beer, and so I thought I better not give any of those guys a beer because if one gets one, the other one will want one, you know, especially when they're all getting antsy knowing they're going into combat. So I drank the rest of it with my buddy on the crew there. And he had duty in the crow's nest one night. And he says, "George, you want to go up on the crow's nest?" I says, "Well, I don't know. That looks pretty scary up there." He says, "Well, you got to climb all the way up on the ladder." And he says, "I'll be up there at a certain time." And he says, "If you want to come up, come on up." He says, "I don't think anybody will see you coming up there." Well, I thought, geez, that would be something to talk home about, you know, so I went up there, and there was just about enough room for him and me. And I had more trouble going down than coming up. And it was scary because the ship was rolling, and I mean it was like being in an amusement park, you know, on some kind of an amusement. I was glad when I got done. That wasn't for me. So, but that was an experience on there. And on my way to Okinawa, I was a very slow reader. I read the whole book of Gone With The Wind. I finished it before we hit the beach. And life on that boat wasn't very exciting. We had two meals a day, and the food wasn't bad on that ship. And then a day or -- Oh, we went to the Carolinas. And I guess we were rendezvousing with the rest of the, the -- what the heck they call that when all the ships are together.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Task force, fleet?

sp.speaker: George Schlee
sp.p: Yeah, the task force. Yeah. They were grouping there, and they let us go ashore on this little island and gave us all some cold beer. We each had two cans of cold beer. So, maybe to make us forget of where we're going. We didn't know where we were going. You know, everybody was guessing. And we thought we were going to Formosa. I mean, you know, just the guys talking. They figure that would probably be a pretty good place to go because we weren't going for Philippines, that was already on its way, and the other islands were already taken, Guam, and Sipan and Tinian, and we weren't even thinking about Okinawa, you know. And we thought, geez, certainly not going to Japan. So a couple days out they told us where we were going, and showed us a map of the island, and they told us about the island, how many troops are on it and what we were going to encounter. And they told us our objectives. They told us about all the other Marine outfits, and the Army outfits, what their objectives were going to be after they hit the beach. I was in the Sixth Marine Division, so we were going to hit the beach. We were going to take the air strip, the Onton (ph) air strip right where we were hitting the beach. It was on the high ground there, and then we were going to sever the island right there, and move south and secure that whole part of Okinawa. And at the end of it like was a mountain called Mount Yarigatake, that was called the Motobu peninsula, and we were supposed to take that mountain. And we were told there were going to be tracks with artillery being run back and forth on these tracks in the mountain because it's honeycombed all the way around. And they told us that every inch of that ground on that island is going to be covered by heavy machine gunfire, mortar fire, artillery fire. The Japs aren't going to miss us. And that was encouraging. So when -- Oh, can I backtrack?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure, yes.

sp.speaker: George Schlee
sp.p: Go back to the Carolinas. We saw an aircraft carrier come in. It must have been going about five knots, very slowly. And it was one of the most moving things I've ever seen during the war. That -- I used to get lumps in my throat when I talked about this, but this aircraft carrier had a hole in it twice the size of your house here. And all the crew or what was left of it were standing at attention on the flight deck in their dress blues. And I don't know whether that was the Roosevelt, and I can't remember where the ship got hit, whether it was in the Coral Sea, or somewhere around -- well, it had to be there some place, but I just don't know, but that was one of the most moving things I ever saw during the war. And all -- We Marines thought that was great. And, okay, now I'm back to getting close to Okinawa. There was nothing, you know, happened aboard ship. I don't even know how many days we were on board ship; a couple weeks I think at least. So we were off the shore of Okinawa in the morning. It was 7 o'clock in the morning. And we were all told to get ready in our outfits, go top side, and go over the nets into our a little LCVPs, bouncing around down there. And they called you off as the units. And when I got top side I couldn't believe what I was seeing. All these ships. Oh, my God, what a mess of ships. And kamikaze planes. I saw the ships getting hit. I saw the ships firing at them, you know, and just before I -- my outfit was called to go down into the -- Could I have a glass of water?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure. All right.

sp.speaker: George Schlee
sp.p: Well, when I got up there at the railing, I was called to go down the net, one kamikaze came swooping down. I don't know that he was coming for us or what, but he landed in the water about maybe a hundred yards away from our boat. Didn't blow up, and we saw him plain as day with his flag wrapped around his head. And we all said, well, that's one guy that isn't going to see his ancestors, he didn't do his job. But that was kind of scary. And that's the only one that I saw going after troop ships. We were surprised. We thought we were going to be targets, you know, we saw all those kamikaze, but they were going after the war ships. And going after LSTs that had the tanks and stuff on them, you know. I guess they figure once they got all the heavy stuff out of the way they could wipe us out once we got ashore. Well, we got in our little boat and as usual, when everybody's going ashore on a strange island, I've seen movies of this too, and it's just like the movies, I guess, that part of it anyway, everybody's anxious, and me and my fox hole buddy, we had a drum of wire, 65 pound drum of wire that we had to carry 'cause they didn't use the radios unless they had to because the Japs would jam them or listen in or something, I don't know, but anyway we had to string wire for telephone. And so we were talking on the way in. And I says, gee, Ralph, I says -- we called one another with our last names and his name was Ralph Halsey. And I says, "Boy, we got a good thing to hit the beach with." I said, "We can hide behind our -- some machine gun opens up, we'll stick this wire in front of us. At least it will help a little." So that was in our favor. So I'm going to back up a second aboard ship. Ralph and I, I don't know where he got the idea, he wanted a haircut, and we only had those little snub nose scissors they give you in a kit. And he says, "George, you cut my hair and I'll cut yours." I says, "Okay." I says, "I don't need a haircut. Japs aren't going to care whether we got a haircut or not." So he didn't do too bad a job on me, but I just butchered him up. I never cut hair before. And he looked in the mirror, and he says, "George, I'm going to kill you." I says, "Well, why don't you let the Japs do that." And boy he hated me. All the way in that's all I heard about was his haircut. That might have been a psychological thing to keep him not thinking about hitting the beach, 'cause -- and he had his helmet on anyway. I says, "Geez, Ralph. Forget it. I said your hair's going to grow back in again." We when got so far from the beach on a destroyer, there's a line of departure they call it, where you can expect fire from, from the beach, machine gun, mortar fire, whatever, you're within range. So the loud speaker yells out and says, "The beach is clear." We thought, holy smokes, no opposition, this is great. And just at that moment our little LCVP gets hung up on the coral reef. We're sitting there at a 30 degree angle. And the swabby there says, "I'm sorry, I can't move, we're stuck on the reef here." He says, "You can't get off." And we says, well, can't you -- Our officer, whoever was in there, we had a lieutenant in charge of our team, says, "Can't you let the gate down?" He says, "No, that's too high for you to jump, you'll hurt yourself, and the coral a sharp." And so we sat there, and watched the kamikazes, you know, for a while hitting the ships out there, and the anti-aircraft bursting in the air there. And finally somehow they got one of these tracks to come along and they unloaded us into that. And it got up there and got us to the beach. Of course, there was no artillery there anyway. We were just with our infantry company that we were attached to. So we lucked out there, and we had no enemy fire. We were the only division on the whole beach of Okinawa that didn't take a beating. The 27th Army Division was, I think they were next to us, and they were getting clobbered, and the 91st Army Division was on the -- hit the beach too. I don't know whether they were next to the 27th or not, but the first Marine Division was in there some place, in between us and the Army -- I mean the Army was in between us and them. Well, anyway, we got up on the -- on the airport, the air strip there. I mean we didn't take it, we just walked up to it, and we dug in. They told us to dig in. And I don't know where the day went. It was dusk before you knew it, and we were still digging fox holes. I don't know what happened, where all the time went that day, to tell you the truth. I know we went ashore at 7 o'clock. I was in the -- We were in the second wave, I think it was, and but anyway, we had a 90 day wonder lieutenant. And we got our fox holes dug, and we got in there, and we start eating our K rations, we had K rations. They're a real meal, it's a real treat. And I think they were K rations from World War I. And mine had worms in it. I had three boxes of K rations in my pack. That's supposed to be a day's rations. And well, of course I couldn't eat it. I just didn't eat it. I opened up the next one, and then I was behind on my rations but that one didn't have worms in it. But I was just wondering whether I was eating worms or not, you know, but anyway all of a sudden a Jap zero lands on the strip, and I don't know whether he didn't know where he was or that we were there or what. It was dusk. It was getting dark. He got out of his plane, and the officers wanted to interrogate him. The guys opened up on him. Oh, geez, they made mince meat out of him, and our officers -- I didn't shoot amount 'cause I didn't even have a loaded weapon, but some of the infantry guys did. And they were -- they were really T'ed off. And I'll try to keep -- I'm not going to use any foul language here.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I've heard some nasty stuff.

sp.speaker: George Schlee
sp.p: Well, I suppose.

sp.speaker: George Schlee
sp.p: But I got used to not talking that way. So, okay. That was our first experience with the enemy. So the next morning the infantry takes off to cut the island in half. And we had a sergeant, our scout sergeant on our team. He had some battle experience previous to going to Okinawa. I think he was at Cape Gloucester in the Solomons. We respected him to no end. And he told us, he says, "The lieutenant's going the wrong way." And, 'cause he knew where we were too because, you know, the scout sergeant has a map and binoculars just like the officer in case he gets hit he could take over. And, of course, the scout sergeant's in charge of the team, basically, to see that they're taken care of and digging their holes and stuff like that, so. And he says, "Guys, I'm not going with him." And the officer says, "I'm telling you guys, let's get going." And the sergeant says, "You know what, guys, our officer doesn't know where our infantry company is. They're gone, they're not even here." And he says, "We got to catch up with them." And it's a good thing there wasn't any enemy there at that particular time. And so the officer took off. He says, "You guys are all going to get court-martialed." And the sergeant says, "Are you guys with me or with him? Go either way you want." And we all said, "We'll go with you, Sarg." We didn't like the lieutenant anyway. So we're walking across the island, and we caught up with the company, the infantry company, and I guess our sergeant talked to the captain of the infantry and he knew we weren't there either, and by that time the artillery had already been on the beach and set up in case we needed them, you know. They were zeroed in already. So the captain says, "Boy, you guys had me worried here." Well, a little while later our lieutenant shows up, and he didn't say anything to us. And the sergeant didn't say anything either. It's best we didn't say anything because he's still a lieutenant. Well, on our way across the island we ran into some pockets of the enemy, and then I think before we got -- I don't know how far we got across the island. I'll tell you that's when I lost track of what was going on because nobody told me anything. All I know, what was going on within a ten-foot square that I was in. I was getting tired of carrying that wire. It was getting heavy. And every time we ran out of wire somebody seemed to find us another one. And a few times I couldn't make it up the hills. Ralph and I were taking turns carrying the -- oh, yeah, we did have an extra roll of wire, and that had to be carried by one man on his shoulders plus your pack. And there were times when I just couldn't make it. And Frenchie, big, husky guy says, "Come on, I'll carry it for you." He didn't have to. Why, I don't know. But Ralph and I were, we were the wire carriers. And so he helped us. And sometimes when the wire would get cut or broken, we had to go back and trouble shoot it. That was scary too, especially when we were in enemy territory, because there were times when the wire got cut by the Japs, and then two guys would have to go back and find where the splice is, and hopefully get back in one piece. Well, we started to engage the heavy part of the enemy there. I experienced some banzai charges at night. They were scary. From what I understand the Japs were saki'ed up. They didn't know where they were going. Sometimes they'd jump right over your fox hole, and the guys would shoot them as they ran over, and it was always at night. Of course, we shot up flares so we could see them, and it was like a field day really. Take your pick. And then the artillery wasn't -- I don't know, I don't remember them calling in our artillery on some of those banzai barrages, advances because it happened so fast. And they were on you in no time, you know, so I guess artillery didn't help. And I guess just the infantry with hand grenades because Marines don't move at night. We do not move. I found that out in both wars. The enemy wants you they got to come and get you at night. We move during the day, I'll swear to that, but not at night. And I think that's -- that's good. And so a lot of them would go past, run past us and get into the rear echelon territory, you know. And our officers, "Well, let the guys back there take care of them, you know, the hell with them. We're just worrying about the guys in front of us," because he says, "You know what, they're not going to come back here and attack us in the rear, they're just going to keep right on going, and surprise those guys back there." I don't know if they talked to them on the telephone, somehow communicated, because there's some on their way, or whatever, I don't know. My first scary, really scary time with a Jap was we were dug in in a yard. I guess it was a yard. There were bushes around where I was, and there was an opening to like a road on the other side of the bushes. And like I said, I never know what's the front line or not. And my lieutenant was -- I was about 15 yards away. My fox hole was about 15 yards away. And I had radio watch that night. The radio was on top, on top of the ground there. And my officer had his foxhole right next to the radio. And my buddy was in his fox hole, and we were told that particular night not to fire our weapons unless it was absolutely necessary. I had no idea what was going on. Well, I was sitting there in my poncho. I had a carbine, that's what I carried. I trained in boot camp with an M-1 and then they gave me a carbine to hit the beach with. And I had my carbine sticking out of my poncho, and I was parallel to the bushes where the opening was. Well, it was real quiet. You could hear machine gun fire every once in a while, or some artillery going off in the distance, but nothing close by. And so I'm sitting there, and out of the corner of my eye I see a head. And I thought that can't be one of our guys. Why would he be moving -- He's not even moving. It just appeared because I was facing this way, and I don't know why I wasn't looking at that opening. I figured, you know, nothing was going on, you know. I felt like we were in reserve or something. So he was inching his way, and I thought, that's a Jap. And he had no pack on or anything, just clothes. I didn't see a sword or a rifle or any -- As he was coming closer I could see that he had -- he was unarmed, as far as I could see. And so I didn't know what to do. I'm not supposed to fire, and I figured if I whip around and try to put a round in him, he's going to get me. And he just -- I don't know how much time went by. It seemed like hours, 'cause he was just inching his way and hardly moving at all. That guy was so well trained that -- and I was just amazed at how slow he was moving. So I finally decided that I'm going to go for this guy. So I did. I whipped around and put a couple of rounds into him, and here all he had was a knife, his dagger. My officer jumped up. He goes, "Schlee, what's going on?" And this is the only time I hit an officer and got away with it. I hit him right in his helmet and said, "Get back in your hole." Because at that very moment that I opened up fire, an ambu machine gun opened up on me, and I took a flying dive into my hole over here, slid right in there. My fox hole buddy made room for me. And then the battle begun. Then we had -- There was a battle with the company. I didn't get to fire any more. I'll tell you, I was scared. I told my buddy, "I'm staying right here." And I had enough for the night. And so I don't -- Evidently we took care of what was out there, the Japs. But the next morning I heard from the infantry company that six or seven of our guys got their throats slit that night. And I thought, well, I'm one of the lucky guys. I don't care if I started a war or not. And -- 'cause I had -- I didn't have that much hand-to-hand training in boot camp. You know, I didn't know how I'd tackle a guy like that, and I wasn't a good boxer or anything, you know, wrestling, never took wrestling in school 'cause I was too skinny. And here I found out later that this was an Imperial Marine, like our rangers, you know and -- raiders. So I felt good about that, that I could tell everybody I killed an Imperial Marine. But before I could even get back to him, the guys all stripped him of his goodies. I got his emblem off his collar and that was about it, and a pin that he had with an anchor on it, and a rope around the anchor, like -- but somebody else got his flag, 'cause every Jap had a flag on him. Well, that was, that was scary. Then -- Is that what you want to hear?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: George Schlee
sp.p: These kind of things?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's exactly.

sp.speaker: George Schlee
sp.p: Okay. Well, all right. When I wasn't on the front lines with the infantry company, and we'd be in reserve, of course, they always put you to work when you're back at the battery where the guns are. Then my MOS was 30 Calgary machine gunner. And a few times I got to -- Frenchie got to be, him and I took turns being machine gunner and assistant gunner. I don't know why they lined me up with him, but then I wasn't with my fox hole buddy anymore. I don't know how they shuffled us around. Sometimes we weren't always together with one another. They give you different jobs. And ole Frenchie, him and I would put up a string of tin cans with the stones in them, in case they tripped them, they'd rattle them and you start peppering them. Frenchie was always trigger happy. "Did you hear that? Did you hear that? Did you hear that?" "I didn't hear anything, I didn't hear anything." He'd cut loose and the company commander would come over, "What the hell you guys doing here? There's no Japs here." And then I'd say, "Well, Frenchie thought he heard something." And then, of course, Frenchie would say, "You heard it too, didn't you?" And I'd say, "yeah, I heard it." Actually we killed no Japs back there with that machine gun, but he got to fire it a few times. My next experience was -- Now, this time when we were at the base of Mount Yarigatake, I'm moving ahead a little bit because in between times there I only had one other experience that probably was different than anybody else. We were more or less in a secured area of some kind. I was in reserve then. And they drove, me and my buddy, to a little hill next to a village, and we were supposed to watch for any unusual things that went on here. And we'd see civilians, but they pointed out in this direction, the enemy's in that direction. I didn't know what we were supposed to be doing, I didn't anyway. Anyway, it was a dull day. And me and my buddy, I don't know whether we were getting sadistic or what, but we saw this one woman down there on the path carrying a bundle on her head. And he says, "You want to make some bets as to which one of us can make her drop that bundle without hitting her?" I said, "I don't care." Well, he had an M-1 and I had my carbine. And we were taking pot shots at her, but she just kept walking, and I don't know, we would hit the bundle, I guess. It looked like we were hitting the bundle, and then we could see some of our shots land in the dirt, but we didn't hit her, but then she started walking faster, and finally started running away, and we thought, well, that wasn't any fun. So later on we saw this civilian walking with a bundle along the rice patty, and my buddy says, "He's going into enemy territory." He says, "He might be carrying some food up to the enemy." We didn't know what he had in there. And he says, "I'll bet you my fruit bar against your fruit bar that I hit him before you do." And he says, "I'll let you take the first shot because you got a carbine." I says, "Okay." Well, I lined him up, and my first shot was short. And my weapon was only sighted for 300 yards, and he could -- he could hit something at 500 easy with his sights and with a muzzle velocity and stuff. So he took his turn, and I saw mine hit in the water, and then the guy started running with his sack the best he could. So I -- My buddy says, "Now I got a moving target." So he took a pot shot at him, and he missed him. We didn't see where his bullet landed. And this was just lucky. I raised the thing. It was a little Kentucky windage, whatever you want to call it, and my sights, way above his head, and I hit him, and I don't know where I hit him but he fell down, and he dropped his sack. And I got the fruit bar, of course, and my buddy says, "Holy smokes", and he says, "Hey, the guy's getting up." I says, "Let him go. He's leaving the sack there. Let him run. He can't be that bad off." He might have got hit in the finger for all we know. So that was another little diddy there that probably nobody's ever done before. See, we call it getting Asiatic over there, we don't call it getting sadistic. I guess you get that way after a while. And then it seems like after a while, and I found this out after when I went to Korea and was up on the front lines again, that -- I shouldn't say this but sometimes it seems like fun to kill somebody, actually. And you put all these notches in your head, not on the stock of your rifle, you know, and you start to feel good about it really. So we got up to the base of Mount Yarigatake, and we were on this hill. I was attached to the Fourth Marines of the -- the Fourth Marine Regimen in the Sixth Marine Division, and a lot of them were raiders because they disbanded the raider battalions because they didn't need them anymore. And I'm telling you, these guys were something else being next to. They had no fear in their hearts at all. I mean all through, even when we crossed the island and stuff, they were amazing. And they could throw a cheese dagger, I'll tell you, and make it hit the target. You you've seen this in the movies, and I've seen guys do this, and not always, you know, have the point sticking where it should, but they hit the target. So I saw one day do it with a railroad spike. I mean he was not throwing it at an enemy, but he hit a piece of wood with it. So anyway, Colonel Shipley was the colonel of that regimen, and for some reason or another he was with Fox Company, the one I was attached to on this particular hill. We encountered some ground forces that day in this -- good old CBs. The one had one of these monster bull dozers, and he protected some of the guys with that blade he had on the front there, and he was taking the brunt of it, but I don't think he got hurt. And I don't -- There weren't very many Japs. I don't know whether they were feeling us out or what, but that didn't last very long. And we did have one of our guys get hit, and he fell down on the far side of the hill, he rolled down there, and nobody volunteered right away to go down there and get him. We didn't know whether he was dead or not. And somebody called for a corpsman, and the corpsman came right away. And he went down there, and I thought, holy smokes, that guy's not even armed, you know. And, well, we watched. I was only a private. I did what I was told. I wasn't going to do anything on my own. And then I had enough problems with the lieutenant, 'cause we still had him yet. And so the guy got hit in the stomach with a bullet. And -- from what I understand, and this corpsman was down there administering something to him. From what I was told he was -- he had a tube of some kind, was sucking something out of his stomach, to keep him -- something from not bleeding or something. I don't know, but anyway he dragged the guy back up there, and I was told he saved his life. He got a medal for that, some kind of a medal. He was decorated. And so that same day we dug in on that knoll, and the next day we were going to attack the base of the mountain. From what I understand, after the war was over that mountain was going to be attacked by us Marines on three sides at the same time, and artillery fire. I know Mount Suribachi on Iwo Jima got a lot of advertisement, and I don't think it was as big a mountain, but because of the flag raising, you know, that's a Marine Corps symbol. And that was -- I appreciate that very much. But this one was honeycomb too. And they had Navy forward observers on our front line there with us trying to knock out the holes in that mountain with 15 inchers. If you ever heard those go over your head, it's something to hear. And, of course, our artillery was trying to pound them with 155 long Toms and howitzers and our little 105s, just barraging the hell out of that mountain. And it was getting hit from all three sides. I don't know whether the 15 inchers were hitting it on the far side because I don't know if the Navy had ships over there or not. But, okay, when they plug up a hole a little while later, just like ants, they been digging out again and they'd started firing -- or, no, they were coming out. They weren't getting a chance to fire. That's what it was. There was a lull in the storm there for some reason or other. I, in my fox hole, dug, for some reason or other I had a fox hole by myself. I don't know whether there was an uneven amount of guys in the team or what. All of a sudden, it was just before dusk again. I don't know why things happened to me at dusk. The artillery started pouring in and mortar barrage. That is the biggest barrage of artillery and mortars that I ever experienced in either or. My fox hole felt like I was in the football field and I was going to die at the age of 19. It was one of the scariest, one of the scariest things I ever went through except when I was decorated, but that was in Korea. That's later on. There was a strange thing that happened to me, and I -- I used to -- I'm going to try not to do it now. I used to break up when I talked about this. And I never told anybody about it till about three years ago at a vet's -- on Veteran's Day, to one of my wife's cousin. He was a corpsman. During the barrage one of the infantryman slid next to my fox hole, and he was Catholic. And he was laying there during the barrage, and he was saying his rosary. And I don't know why I said this to him. I was so dammed scared. I says, "Would you say a prayer for me?" And, gee, I have a hard time over this one. The minute I said that, a shell landed on the other side of him and took half his head off. And I had to get out of my hole. I couldn't stand to look at him. And right away, I mean during -- the barrage was still on yet. I was told to help the wounded off the hill and the dead. I was ordered to do that. So me and another guy, we -- we was given a stretcher, and we took our first guy. It was dark then, there was no light. And so we had to walk down that hill on that rocky coral, and we stumbled with him and dropped him, and he would money and groan. And I think by the time we got him down there he was dead, he wasn't even alive anymore. So they sent us back up for some -- another one. And we were feeling our way around. I didn't even know who was helping me. I lost track of everybody. And so I did that about three times. And then they said, "Don't go back up anymore." Because Colonel Shipley, I remember him, when the barrage started he was right up on top of the hill there, and he was telling everybody to get off; "Get off this hill", you know, "the best way you can." So he -- I don't know why he didn't get hit. He was standing up there like nobody's business. And so later on, I don't know how I got back to my battery, where the guns were. I wasn't hit, fortunately. Our lieutenant had the whole team up for court-martial again because they weren't -- he didn't know where they were. Isn't that dumb? So I told the captain. I said -- I told him what I was doing. And so the captain, he said -- He called the lieutenant up over to his Jeep, I guess back there, and that was his headquarters, a Jeep. And so he chewed him out, I guess. He didn't want to do it in front of everybody, and tried to tell him what we were all doing for Pete's sakes, and I guess he asked him what he was doing. So that all worked out pretty good. But I had a problem with that incident. I still have it today. I get flash backs continuously. I'm taking therapy at the VA because of that, and seeing a psychiatrist every three months. So -- Where was I? Oh, yeah. So when I got back in reserve I went to see the chaplain, and I had to talk to him about this. And I considered myself a Christian. You know, I went to church. I was in the Boy Scouts in church and stuff. In fact, I was even a Boy Scout chaplain. And that bugged me to end, that guy took the -- got hit when I said something like that to him. Well, the chaplain says, "Private," he says, "what were you thinking about? Why did you ask him to say a prayer for you? Were you asking for a prayer to save your neck?" And I -- I said, "I don't know, chaplain." I said, "I was scared." And he says, "Well I'll bet you that's what you were doing, weren't you?" I mean he was giving me the works there. And I says, "Yeah, I guess I was." He says, "Well, that was the wrong thing to ask for." He says, "How many other guys on that hill were asking the same thing here or would be?" He said nobody -- He says, "You mean God was going to save all you guys and just let you walk off that hill?" He says, "Don't work that way." So, I can't remember what he all said to me, but he got me calmed down to the point where I was okay, but, of course, I would never forget it. And I even mentioned it -- No, I never did tell anybody about that, that's right. I used to tell them about other things. I used to be a Sunday school teacher after I got out, and I used to relate some of the problems I had during the war, but I never told them about that one. Where am I? Okay. Mount Yarigatake. Well, we secured the island -- We took our three objectives. We finally took the island, or that portion of it. The 27th -- Did I say 24th or 27th.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: 27th.

sp.speaker: George Schlee
sp.p: I get mixed up with that too. Anyway, they were still on the beach after we were fighting for a couple of weeks, I guess, I think it was. They put us in reserve 'cause our objection, we could still see -- They put us in a place where we could see some of the anti-aircraft fire from off shore, and the Betty bombers going over at night, with the spotlights on them, trying to knock them down. And we thought, well, our part of the war is over with. Well, we weren't there more than, I don't know, a day or two, we didn't even get any beer, and they says, "Pack up, you're moving out." We weren't too happy about that either. And I found out we had to take over the Army's positions, and down there where Sugar Loaf Hill was. And so that was an ordeal in itself, trying to take over -- I guess from what I hear, the minute we took over we advanced at least 500 yards. We took a beating, but we moved. And that was the dumbest thing they could have done was sit there and get the hell beaten out of them. I mean you just don't do that. And I've seen it happen so much with the Army, that's why I have an attitude against them. I saw it a lot in Korea. So, well, we took -- I didn't -- I wasn't in on Sugar Loaf Hill. My company didn't engage in that. We went to a Orocco (ph) peninsula, and that's where we saw these civilians and people jumping off the cliff killing themselves. They wouldn't surrender. That was an experience. And they just wouldn't do it. Boy, they grabbed their kids and take them and jump right off. And some of the enemies killed themselves, shot themselves. This is funny. The one day there I saw a nice pair of hot nail boots on the foot a Jap sticking in the ground there. He was covered up. From his knees on up his legs were sticking out of the ground. I thought, boy, those things look new, and I put my foot up there, and I said, those are my size. So I thought, well, he can't be booby trapped, just his legs are sticking up. So I untied the boots and went to pull one of them, and everything came with it, from the knee down. And, of course, I didn't take the boots, I wasn't going to scrape them out with a spoon, so that was a weird experience. One time our FO team on Okinawa caught a donkey, and we -- Life magazine took our picture. We loaded our radio and all our stuff on the donkey, and, of course, he only lasted for a couple of days and got cholera and died on us, but that was an experience. And one time the Life magazine, they had cameras and everything. They were interviewing guys on tape, and sending the messages back home. And they got this one guy and ask him how he was, and he says, "Would you like to say a few words back home?" And he just yelled in the microphone, "Get me the hell out of here." And that was it. I mean he yelled. Probably broke the microphone. That was funny. So we stayed on that island and knocked off a hundred thousand Japs, I understand, in a little less than three months. And then we went -- Oh, we experienced a typhoon there, and there wasn't action going on then. The mud was knee deep, and some of the lighter ships were heaved ashore, and that was another experience. And I can't think of anything else anybody would want to hear. Oh, I brought back an ambu machine gun that I found. I didn't capture it. I found it on Okinawa and I managed to bring it back. Beautiful. Their machine guns were better than ours. They spit out more rounds than ours. You could tell one when of theirs was firing against one of ours, that's one way you could tell. And so I didn't know what to do with it. You weren't allowed to go back to the states with it, you know. And we were getting ready to go to war again somewhere. And so I sold it to one of the cooks. And he said, "What do you want for it?" I said, "Well, give me 300 bucks for it." And he bought it. And 300 bucks back then was a lot of money. Then, of course, we found out Japan was bombed with the atom bomb and the war was going to be over with, so that was the end of all the fun. I -- After that they shipped our division to Tsingtao, China, to get the Japs out of there and send back home. I spent six months there, but that was nice liberty. One night me and my buddy was out on liberty, and we saw this, these Chinese soldiers mauling up this little Jap. So we went over and told the chinks to lay off. I mean they were afraid of us, deathly afraid of us, even though they were on our side. And so we ask him where he lived, he could speak English. He said up on the hill there. And so, okay, we'll take you home. So here he takes us to, geez, a real classy neighborhood there with the stone wall around the house and an iron gate, and dogs on the other side barking their head off. And a guy comes, opens up the gate, and, of course, he says, we helped him up there. And his brother's name was Masaki Izumi (ph). So he says, come on in. Gee, helping my brother, an American, holy smokes. And so he let us into -- he took us in the home, and, holy smokes, they had a nice place. Even had one room all decorated in American furniture. The rest was all mats and stuff, you know sit on the floor, low furniture. And we were just a couple of privates, and treated us to some food and saki, of course. And we couldn't walk a straight line after we left there. Good thing our compound was only a couple blocks away. But that guy couldn't do enough for me and my buddy the whole six months we were there, believe me. He even had a Christmas tree decorated for us on Christmas, invited us over there. Isn't that something? And we talked about the wars and stuff, and he was a captain in the Japanese ortori (ph). He was a college graduate. He owned stock in the Mitsubishi factory. I showed him a Life magazine of what was left of his factory, and he wasn't too happy about that. I guess he didn't know it. One time he got a little angry, but he held himself back; when we were sitting on the floor and opened a page and Hirohito was sitting on his white horse in a picture in Life magazine, and he didn't like that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: ____(1 second)?

sp.speaker: George Schlee
sp.p: Yeah. He didn't like us looking down at him either. And so we -- what did he with know, you know, but, of course, he kept it cool. But here we found out that he was the head honcho of all the Japs in the city that; that he was the only one of the -- Every Jap in that city was allowed to carry a pistol to protect themselves and keep the war dogs. Isn't it something to meet somebody like that? END OF CD.
